meta.worktree: Fictional demonstration — no real source was inspected
meta.scope: Fictional commerce platform · customer, operations, and reporting flows

summary.verdict: Protect customer boundaries first. Then make payments and stock updates recoverable, with focused changes to the existing system.
executive: Customers browse products, place orders, and receive payment receipts. Operations staff use a separate workspace to investigate orders and review sales.
One confirmed high-priority access-control problem allows an authenticated customer to retrieve another account’s order. Address that boundary before the next release.
Validate the payment retry risk and fix the worker’s lost-update behavior. Together these affect payment confidence, customer-visible status, and support recovery.
Stock cache invalidation is inconsistent, while catalog queries and large exports need scale validation. A narrow fix and targeted measurements are more useful than a rewrite.
This sample contains 12 capabilities and 8 findings. Five problems are confirmed within the fictional scenario; three remain conditional risks. Review gaps remain visible.
architecture: The customer portal serves shoppers, while the operations workspace supports the internal team. Shared application services handle identity, orders, and product browsing.
Orders and products are stored in the primary database. A stock cache speeds up catalog browsing; a reporting store supports the team’s sales view. Those stores have different freshness expectations.

The payment platform sends events to a background worker, which updates orders and requests a receipt. Hosting and reporting replication are inferred boundaries; the map marks those connections with dashed lines.

strengths.description: The example centralizes payment-provider access behind one adapter. Keep that boundary: it gives retry and validation changes a focused home.

evidence.note: Illustrative adapter boundary; this file is fictional.

assumptions: Effort assumes one engineer familiar with this fictional platform, including focused tests and review.
Customer accounts are intended to be isolated. Production configuration has not been inspected.
questions: Does the payment provider enforce idempotency through configuration or a layer absent from this example?
What release capacity and operational ownership are available for the background worker?
What catalog size and export volume should the platform support at peak usage?
How fresh must stock availability and sales reports be for customers and the operations team?

findings.title: Customers can retrieve another account’s order
findings.severity_reason: An authenticated customer can cross an account boundary using a known order identifier; the example route has no ownership check.
findings.description: In the fictional route, authentication is required, but retrieval uses only the order identifier. The repository query and response path contain no account constraint.

evidence.note: Fictional handler returns the lookup result after checking only that a session exists.
Fictional query selects by order ID without account ownership.

findings.technical_impact: The missing account predicate permits cross-account read access. This establishes an unsafe code path, not evidence that a real incident occurred.
findings.business_impact: Customer order information can be disclosed to another account, undermining customer trust and increasing support and incident-response work.
findings.recommendation: Constrain the query to both order ID and authenticated account ID. Return the normal not-found response for inaccessible orders and add cross-account regression tests.

effort.assumptions: Includes route and repository tests; assumes no exceptional shared-order policy or data migration.

findings.verification: Account A can read its own order; account B receives no order data for the same ID. Test both direct route access and repository behavior.

findings.title: Retried payment requests may create duplicate charges
findings.severity_reason: Duplicate payments would materially affect a core business flow, but provider-level protection and actual retry behavior have not been established.
findings.description: The fictional adapter sends payment creation without a stable idempotency key. A caller retry after a timeout could create another payment if the provider does not deduplicate it.

evidence.note: Fictional request payload includes no stable request key; provider settings are outside the inspected scope.

findings.technical_impact: A timeout can leave the original request outcome unknown. Repeating it may create a second provider-side operation.
findings.business_impact: If the risk is reachable, customers may need refunds and support may need to reconcile duplicate payments.
findings.recommendation: First validate provider deduplication and caller retries. If protection is absent, derive a stable payment-attempt key and persist the provider result for safe retry.

effort.assumptions: Includes validation and adapter regression tests; provider sandbox access is available; excludes refunds or historical data cleanup.

findings.verification: Confirm provider settings, then replay the same logical payment after an induced timeout in an isolated test. Verify that at most one payment is created.

findings.title: Failed payment updates disappear without recovery
findings.severity_reason: A bounded worker failure loses a payment update and creates manual recovery work; broad outage or financial loss is not established.
findings.description: The fictional payment worker catches a database exception, emits no useful diagnostic event, and acknowledges the message as successfully handled.

evidence.note: Fictional catch block suppresses the error and completes the callback without retry.

findings.technical_impact: A transient storage error can permanently leave order status stale because the event is acknowledged before the update succeeds.
findings.business_impact: Customers can see an incorrect order status and support staff must investigate and repair affected orders manually.
findings.recommendation: Acknowledge only after a successful update. Use bounded retries and a recoverable failure queue, with a correlation ID and redacted diagnostic logging.

effort.assumptions: Includes failure-path tests and operational instructions; assumes retry support in the existing event infrastructure.

findings.verification: Inject a transient database failure. Verify bounded retry, successful eventual update, and a visible recoverable state when retries are exhausted.

findings.title: Releases can bypass the existing test suite
findings.severity_reason: The example release job lacks a test gate. This permits regressions to reach release, though no deployed regression is claimed.
findings.description: The fictional release workflow builds and publishes directly. The repository already defines a test command, but the release job does not invoke it or depend on a successful test job.

evidence.note: Fictional release steps build and deploy without a test dependency.
Fictional manifest defines an existing test command.

findings.technical_impact: A buildable change can be published even if its behavioral tests fail. Static workflow inspection does not establish branch protection in the live platform.
findings.business_impact: Avoidable regressions can interrupt customer ordering and increase rollback and support effort.
findings.recommendation: Gate the release job on the existing behavioral test command. Add the cross-account and payment failure cases from the earlier phases; validate branch protection separately.

effort.assumptions: Existing tests run in CI without production credentials; excludes broad test-suite repair.

findings.verification: In an isolated CI trial, a deliberately failing behavioral test prevents release; a passing run can proceed.

findings.title: Stock changes leave the customer cache stale
findings.severity_reason: A mismatched cache key prevents the intended refresh after an order. The impact is bounded by the cache expiry; no overselling incident is claimed.
findings.description: The catalog reads stock under a product-scoped key. The order service invalidates a different key, so the existing customer-facing value survives the update.

evidence.note: Illustrative read key uses stock:product:{id}.
Illustrative invalidation uses stock:{id}, which does not match the read key.

findings.technical_impact: The cached availability remains stale until expiry even though the order has changed the underlying stock record.
findings.business_impact: Customers can see availability that has already changed, causing failed checkout attempts and avoidable support questions.
findings.recommendation: Centralize the existing cache-key construction and invalidate the exact product key after the stock transaction commits.

effort.assumptions: Includes a read-update-read regression test; assumes the current cache supports exact-key deletion.

findings.verification: Warm the stock cache, complete an order, and fetch availability again. Verify the updated value is returned without waiting for expiry.

findings.title: Large product lists may trigger repeated stock queries
findings.severity_reason: The query pattern grows with product count, but realistic catalog sizes and measured latency are not available.
findings.description: The illustrative listing loads products and then awaits a stock lookup for each item. This may create excessive database round trips at larger catalog sizes.

evidence.note: Illustrative loop performs an awaited stock lookup for each product.

findings.technical_impact: The number of round trips can grow with the number of displayed products. Caching, query planning, and the real page size could reduce the impact.
findings.business_impact: If this becomes a bottleneck, customers may wait longer to browse and the database may have less capacity for checkout traffic.
findings.recommendation: Measure query count and response time at the expected page size. If material, fetch stock for the selected products in one bounded batch.

effort.assumptions: Includes measurement and a focused batching change only if needed; excludes broad database redesign.

findings.verification: Measure representative small and peak catalog pages in an isolated environment. Compare query count and response time before deciding on remediation.

findings.title: Sales exports may exceed safe memory limits
findings.severity_reason: The export collects all selected records in memory, but the actual data volume and hosting limits have not been verified.
findings.description: The example export handler collects all reporting rows and builds a complete CSV string before sending a response. It does not impose an explicit export-size bound.

evidence.note: Illustrative export loads all selected rows and joins one in-memory CSV.

findings.technical_impact: Memory use and processing time grow with the selected history. The path may hit process or request-duration limits at scale.
findings.business_impact: If the risk is reachable, team members may be unable to obtain large reports and retrying exports may consume capacity needed by other work.
findings.recommendation: Establish expected export volume and runtime limits. Add a bounded selection or a streamed export, choosing the smaller change that meets the actual need.

effort.assumptions: Includes a volume check and focused export change; excludes a new reporting platform or scheduled export service.

findings.verification: Exercise the expected maximum export in an isolated environment, recording memory and completion time. Confirm clear handling of requests beyond supported bounds.

findings.title: Setup instructions name a retired payment setting
findings.severity_reason: A concrete setup mismatch creates local onboarding friction. Production misconfiguration or service interruption is not established.
findings.description: The illustrative setup guide tells a developer to set PAYMENT_KEY, while startup reads PAYMENT_API_KEY. Following the documented steps leaves the required setting absent.

evidence.note: Illustrative setup names the retired PAYMENT_KEY setting.
Illustrative startup reads PAYMENT_API_KEY.

findings.technical_impact: A developer following the guide cannot start the payment integration without investigating the environment validation error.
findings.business_impact: New contributors lose time on setup and need help from someone who knows the configuration history.
findings.recommendation: Update the documented setting and example environment file to match the current startup contract.

effort.assumptions: Documentation and example configuration update only; no credential rotation is implied.

findings.verification: Follow the documented setup in a disposable environment using placeholder sandbox credentials and verify the variable name matches startup validation.

roadmap.title: Protect customer boundaries
roadmap.goal: Close the demonstrated cross-account read path with a narrow correction and a behavioral regression test.
success_criteria: Cross-account order reads return no customer data.
Own-account reads continue to work and are covered by tests.

roadmap.title: Make payments recoverable
roadmap.goal: Validate the duplicate-payment risk and ensure failed updates remain visible and safely recoverable.
success_criteria: Payment retry behavior is demonstrated in an isolated environment.
Repeated logical requests produce at most one payment, if remediation is required.
Transient worker failures retry and exhausted failures remain recoverable.
Customer-visible stock refreshes immediately after a successful order.

roadmap.title: Keep fixes in place
roadmap.goal: Protect the corrected behaviors in release checks, validate the catalog and export limits, and make setup instructions accurate.
success_criteria: A failing behavioral test blocks release.
Release ownership and rollback instructions are clear.
Catalog and export behavior meets a documented representative workload.
The setup guide uses the configuration expected by startup.
